title: Choreographed SDK mini-lab templates — daily journal
content:
Purpose:
A compact, repeatable set of tiny, instructor-less SDK labs that a new engineer or integrator can complete in 20–40 minutes. Focus: frictionless first requests, visible telemetry, and repeatable failure modes so we can iterate on docs + SDK ergonomics quickly.

Audience:
- New SDK adopters (engineers, PMs who will demo)
- Solutions engineers running short customer workshops
- Internal onboarding for new hires on the DevExp team

Design principles (short bullets):
- Choreographed: each lab is a script + expected outputs so non-experts can run it.
- Observable: every step has a single telemetry assertion to check that the SDK behaved as expected.
- Recoverable: teach a small set of quick recovery steps (token leak, network fail, invalid schema).
- Modular: labs composed as building blocks (auth, simple generation, streaming, embeddings, batch).
- Low setup: CLI-friendly, single env var for creds, minimal OS deps.
- Measurable: collect time-to-first-token and success rates.

Structure of a single mini-lab (template):
1) "Quick context" (1–2 lines): why this lab exists
2) "Prep" (1–2 shell commands): env var and install
3) "Scripted steps" (3–6 numbered steps) with exact commands to run
4) "What success looks like" (text + sample output snippet)
5) "Telemetry checkpoint" (metric name + expected range)
6) "Failure injection" (one or two quick fault scenarios and expected recovery)
7) "Notes for facilitator / automation" (optional)

Three starter labs (short outlines) — these are intentionally different from our existing quickstarts:
A) "Hello stream — first-token choreography" (20–25m)
- Quick context: prove streaming works end-to-end and surface client buffering behavior.
- Prep: pip install redwood-sdk; export REDWOOD_API_KEY=xxx
- Steps:
  1. Run minimal Python script that opens a streaming generation and prints tokens as they arrive.
  2. Run the same with NETWORK_DELAY=200ms to force chunking and compare token cadence.
  3. Open the Console trace for the request id and verify event timestamps.
- Success: first token arrives < 400ms in baseline; tokens stream, not batched into a single chunk. Sample output: "t: Hello"
- Telemetry: first_token_latency_ms (baseline < 400), stream_chunk_count (>1 for delayed case)
- Failure injection: 1) Simulate dropped connection (ctrl-C mid-stream) and confirm client receives a partial-result error and the Console shows a canceled state. Recovery: retry with small backoff.

B) "Embed & recall — 3-step memory test" (30–40m)
- Quick context: validate embedder output stability and a simple approximate-recall search using local vector store (instructions for sqlite-backed store).
- Prep: npm install @redwood/embed-client; yarn build-sample-store
- Steps:
  1. Embed three short documents and save vectors to local sqlite.
  2. Query semantic similarity for a held-out prompt and verify the top-1 is the expected doc id.
  3. Run with reduced model (cheaper) to show quality regression.
- Success: cosine(top1, query) >= 0.75 for baseline model; degrade by 0.1 when switching to quantized model (expected).
- Telemetry: embed_invoke_tokens, embed_call_success_rate, vector_store_hit_rate
- Failure injection: corrupt one embedding row and run a repair script. Notes: include SQL snippet to reindex.

C) "Roll-forward canary — SDK feature flag + fallback" (25–35m)
- Quick context: show how to opt a route into a canary model via a single SDK flag and validate fallback path when model unavailable.
- Prep: set REDWOOD_NEXT_FLAG=true; curl to toggle remote flag API (dev-only)
- Steps:
  1. Call the generation API with feature_flag=next_lang_model and confirm returned model_id is the canary variant.
  2. Force a simulated OOM on the canary backend (dev harness) and confirm the SDK falls back to a pinned stable variant and surface a routed_event in telemetry.
  3. Inspect per-request cost breakdown in Console for both runs.
- Success: request succeeds and cost delta is visible; fallback path logged and request latency within SLO *after* fallback.
- Telemetry: routed_model_variant, fallback_triggered_bool, post_fallback_latency_ms
- Failure injection: mis-set flag -> SDK should raise clear error with hint: "invalid flag name".

Automation and facilitator notes (how to run at scale):
- Each lab has a "session.json" artifact (small) created by the run script that contains: request_ids, timestamps, pass/fail, notable telemetry values. This can be uploaded to S3 for batch analysis.
- Provide a one-click harness for CI that runs all labs in 10–12m using minimal mocks (stub streaming, fake vector store) so we can gate SDK PRs for regressions.
- Fast-check CLI: redwood-mini-lab run --name=hello-stream --collect=session.json

Telemetry checklist (minimal set to add to SDKs):
- request_id (span)
- client_version
- first_token_latency_ms
- total_tokens_generated
- model_id_requested and model_id_served
- feature_flags_used (list)
- fallback_reason (enum)

Developer-facing success metrics (what we measure to consider this onramp good):
- median time-to-first-token (TTFT) for Hello-Stream < 600ms across regions
- embed_top1_recall >= 0.7 on our sample corpus
- canary fallback success rate > 99% when backend fails
- lab completion rate (new users) >= 80% within 40m without facilitator

Open questions / TODOs (short-running):
- Do we want a single repo that contains all run-harnesses (scripts + session uploader) or split by language? pros/cons for discoverability.
- Decide whether session artifacts include raw text (PII risk) — default to redaction but need per-lab opt out. (Action: Priya to draft policy).
- Instrument SDK to emit feature_flags_used in first pass (Liam to pick up).
- Add a web-based runner that sequences labs for non-terminal users — priority: low.

Quick checklist for doc authoring (one-liners):
- [ ] Write full step-by-step for Hello-Stream with code samples in Python/Node.
- [ ] Add sample session.json schema and uploader script.
- [ ] Add SQL repair snippet for Embed lab.
- [ ] Add sample Console links (placeholders currently) and a short video capture script for replay.

Notes to self (voicey):
- Keep examples tiny. People bail when they see a 200-line sample. Small wins: a single curl + a single python snippet.
- Use real request IDs in sample outputs (no secrets) so troubleshooting steps map directly to Console UI.

Session history (journal entries):
- 2025-11-20: initial outline — sketched three labs, gathered a4 sample telemetry fields.
- 2025-12-02: PoC harness that runs Hello-Stream with a stub streaming server (works end-to-end).
- 2026-01-15: ran pilot with Solutions Eng (5 ppl) — observed confusion around env var names and the streaming buffer behavior.
- 2026-02-28: updated telemetry checklist and added canary-fallback lab notes.

References / links (internal):
- Feature flagging RFC: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DEV/Feature+Flagging+RFC
- Telemetry contract v0.2: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OBS/SDK+Telemetry+Schema+v0.2
- Linear: DEVEXP-233 (mini-lab harness infra)

Last quick thought: keep the "daily journal" rolling inside this doc. I want a one-paragraph daily note at the top when something changes so we can chronologically see edits without digging into version history.

-- Maya
